claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 12:12–12:22 in which the driver covered 6.47 km where the optimal route covers 1.32 km, adding 5.15 km and straying up to 1194 m from the optimal route; under RD-1 this unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route is an unexempted detour segment.

RydeTAXI is metered, so the extra 5.15 km of the unexempted segment directly entered the fare; RD-2 therefore awards refund_partial of 5.15 km × the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (fare distance $20.43 ÷ 14.5 km) = $7.26 SGD.

No traffic exemption applies: there were no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window (F12), and the only congestion records are speed bands 4 and 5 (30–49 km/h), not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires and which in any case cannot exempt a segment on its own.

The chat record contains no route-change proposal by the driver before the deviation and no rider agreement: the only messages are the rider's location note and the driver's arrival note, both at 12:03, nine minutes before the off-route segment started at 12:12, so RD-5 consent cannot be found for that segment.

The driver's statement that he simply followed GPS is not a reasonable cause under RD-4, which requires traffic evidence for the replaced portion of the optimal route, and it is contradicted by the system records showing a 5.15 km detour with no incident nearby.

Because the deviation is upheld, RD-6's precondition for a flag_account referral on the driver is not met — the profile shows the driver has 0 upheld disputes in 90 days and the rider's own 2 upheld route disputes concern the rider's history, not the driver's.

weaknesses: The gps facts put the detour at +5.15 km (F3) while the fare fact bills excess distance of 5.9 km (F4/F1); the difference of ~0.75 km is map-matching residual, so the driver will argue the whole excess distance should be compared against the optimal route rather than the single segment — under RD-2 only the unexempted segment's extra_km is refundable, and any residual above the segment sum is not.

The driver will cite F9 ('I followed my GPS; it rerouted me') and F10/F11 (speed bands 4 and 5 on Ayer Rajah Expressway and Jurong Town Hall Road during 11:57–12:33) to argue there was a reasonable cause to reroute, even though RD-4 requires an incident (F12 shows none) and bands 4–5 fall far outside the band 1–2 severe-congestion threshold.
The rider's own profile (F14) shows 2 upheld route disputes in 90 days, which the other side may use to suggest a pattern of fare complaints.
RD-2's per-km rate is derived from the fare facts ($20.43 ÷ 14.5 km = $1.41/km, F6), and Ryde publishes no official refund formula (policy gap G5), so the exact quantum is open to challenge.
The chat evidence (F7, F8) is thin — it shows no agreement but also no explicit refusal, so absence of consent must be inferred from the system timestamps in F3.

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $7.26 (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (F6), so distance actually driven enters the fare, unlike the fixed-quote services [RD-2]. The system records show a single off-route segment 12:12–12:22 in which 6.47 km was driven where the optimal route covers 1.32 km, adding 5.15 km and straying up to 1194 m from the optimal route [F3]; total actual distance 14.5 km versus 8.6 km optimal (+5.9 km, +69%) [F1]. Under RD-1 any such unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route is an unexempted detour segment [RD-1].

No exemption applies. RD-4 requires a traffic incident on the replaced stretch of the optimal route: no incidents were recorded near the route during the trip window [F12]. The only congestion records are speed bands 4 and 5 (30–39 and 40–49 km/h) on Ayer Rajah Expressway and Jurong Town Hall Road [F10][F11], which are not the band 1–2 severe congestion of RD-4(b) and, in any case, cannot exempt a segment on their own [RD-4]. Weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain [F13], so no environmental cause arises under RD-4. The driver's statement that his GPS rerouted him [F9] is a statement, and the system records [F3][F12] override it; a GPS instruction is not the traffic evidence RD-4 demands [RD-4].

RD-5 mutual agreement also fails: the chat contains only the rider's 12:03 location note and the driver's 12:03 arrival note [F7][F8], nine minutes before the segment began at 12:12 [F3], with no route-change proposal by the driver before leaving the optimal route and no rider agreement [RD-5]. claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 12:12–12:22 in which the driver covered 6.47 km where the optimal route covers 1.32 km, adding 5.15 km and straying up to 1194 m from the optimal route; under RD-1 this unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route is an unexempted detour segment.

RydeTAXI is metered, so the extra 5.15 km of the unexempted segment directly entered the fare; RD-2 therefore awards refund_partial of 5.15 km × the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (fare distance $20.43 ÷ 14.5 km) = $7.26 SGD.

No traffic exemption applies: there were no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window (F12), and the only congestion records are speed bands 4 and 5 (30–49 km/h), not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires and which in any case cannot exempt a segment on its own.

The chat record contains no route-change proposal by the driver before the deviation and no rider agreement: the only messages are the rider's location note and the driver's arrival note, both at 12:03, nine minutes before the off-route segment started at 12:12, so RD-5 consent cannot be found for that segment.

The driver's statement that he simply followed GPS is not a reasonable cause under RD-4, which requires traffic evidence for the replaced portion of the optimal route, and it is contradicted by the system records showing a 5.15 km detour with no incident nearby.

Because the deviation is upheld, RD-6's precondition for a flag_account referral on the driver is not met — the profile shows the driver has 0 upheld disputes in 90 days and the rider's own 2 upheld route disputes concern the rider's history, not the driver's.

weaknesses: The gps facts put the detour at +5.15 km (F3) while the fare fact bills excess distance of 5.9 km (F4/F1); the difference of ~0.75 km is map-matching residual, so the driver will argue the whole excess distance should be compared against the optimal route rather than the single segment — under RD-2 only the unexempted segment's extra_km is refundable, and any residual above the segment sum is not.

The driver will cite F9 ('I followed my GPS; it rerouted me') and F10/F11 (speed bands 4 and 5 on Ayer Rajah Expressway and Jurong Town Hall Road during 11:57–12:33) to argue there was a reasonable cause to reroute, even though RD-4 requires an incident (F12 shows none) and bands 4–5 fall far outside the band 1–2 severe-congestion threshold.
The rider's own profile (F14) shows 2 upheld route disputes in 90 days, which the other side may use to suggest a pattern of fare complaints.
RD-2's per-km rate is derived from the fare facts ($20.43 ÷ 14.5 km = $1.41/km, F6), and Ryde publishes no official refund formula (policy gap G5), so the exact quantum is open to challenge.
The chat evidence (F7, F8) is thin — it shows no agreement but also no explicit refusal, so absence of consent must be inferred from the system timestamps in F3.

claims.assertion: Only one off-route segment exists, 12:12–12:22, in which 6.47 km was driven where the optimal route covers 1.32 km, adding 5.15 km; the remainder of the excess distance (5.9 km total per the GPS track) is not attributable to any second unexamined deviation.
The driver's written statement is that he followed the GPS reroute, and the GPS track shows a single continuous off-route segment, i.e. no unexplained extra detours beyond that one segment.

The traffic record shows no incident, roadwork or blockage at all near the route during the trip window, so the driver cannot invoke the RD-4(a) reasonable-cause exemption for the off-route segment; no traffic incident fact supports the reroute.

The only congestion records are speed bands 4 and 5 (30–39 and 40–49 km/h), which are not band 1 or 2, and even band 1/2 alone would not be sufficient for exemption under the MVP rule; the reroute therefore remains an unexempted segment.
The chat log contains no message from the rider requesting or agreeing to any routing change before the deviation began, so the RD-5 mutual-agreement defence is unavailable to the driver.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (metered total $31.56 including a $20.43 distance component at $1.41/km), so the fare tracks distance and the excess km can be refunded per the metered-fare branch of RD-2; the refundable amount is the single unexempted segment's extra 5.15 km × $1.41/km = $7.26, well below the billed excess of $8.35.

The driver pressed no waiting-fee charge (waiting $0.00) and collected no extra item; the dispute is confined to the mileage of the single segment, so there is no basis for any further penalty or fee correction in this case.
The driver's 90-day record shows zero upheld route disputes and no prior route finding, so the RD-6 'repeated' account flag does not apply to this case.

The rider's own 90-day record shows two upheld route complaints, which means the rider is a repeat complainant on route issues; this is context only and does not reduce the driver's liability for the single unexempted segment.

weaknesses: F1 and F3 are adverse to the driver: the GPS shows 14.5 km actual vs 8.6 km optimal (+5.9 km, +69%) with a 6.47 km off-route segment adding 5.15 km, which is an unexempted deviation under RD-1 — the driver cannot defeat the route finding itself.

F9 (driver's statement 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me') is a statement only, and RD-4 requires traffic evidence rather than a GPS explanation; F12 records no traffic incident near the route, so no reasonable-cause exemption is available.

F4 shows the billing already charged the full 5.9 km excess at $1.41/km ($8.35), so the meter overcharge on the segment is real and a refund of about $7.26 for the 5.15 km segment is hard to resist; the only arguable reduction is that the residual 0.75 km is map-matching residual (≤ 0.25 km guidance is exceeded), which is a weak mitigation at best.

F10 and F11 (bands 4 and 5 on Ayer Rajah Expressway and Jurong Town Hall Road) show the roads were moving at 30–49 km/h, which weakens any claim that severe congestion forced the detour, and F12's absence of incidents leaves the driver without RD-4 cover.
